messages.subject: Sampling lagging/stopping during execution
parts:
When executing stan, the iterations lag/hang around the 400 mark. I've specified only a limited amount of parameters to save, thinned the samples and still it won't move. I notice that the warm up stage moves quite fast and then gets slower and slower as the iteration progress until it eventually hangs.

I'm trying to reproduce the analysis in http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?arnumber=7173066 but using HMC methods as to avoid the requirement for conjugacy.  The general gist is that the degradation data is provided for a Li-ion battery, with capacitance decreasing over time. The voltage-discharge curves are fit with a spline using a single knot, the location of which is itself a parameter. The sampler runs fine when I just look at the first 10 discharge profiles, however when I incorporate all 168 lines it stuffs up.

My Stan model is:

```
data{
  int<lower=1> J;               // Number of groups
  int<lower=1> N;               // Number of points
  int<lower=1> C;               // Number of covariates in theta
  int<lower=1> K;               // Number of gammas
  int<lower=1, upper=J> jj[N];  // Individual indicator of group (integer reading out of vector of length N)
  vector[N] times;              // Time intercept variables for each point
  vector[N] U;                  // Voltage measurement for each point
  matrix[C,K] C_j[J];            // Array of design matricies for each point
}


parameters {
  cholesky_factor_corr[C] L;    // Hyperprior correlation matrix
  vector<lower=0>[C] scale;     // Hyperprior scale matrix for covariance
  vector[K] gamma;              // Hyperprior for the theta means in terms of gamma. This is resolved down to a vector of length C with the design matrix C_j
  real<lower=0> sigma;          // Noise parameter
  matrix[J,C] theta;            // Individual group coefficents (reads vector length K from a vector of length J)
}


transformed parameters {
  vector[J] a0;                 // Theta parameters
  vector[J] a1;
  vector[J] a2;
  vector[J] a3;
  vector[J] b3;
  vector[J] tau;
  
  vector[J] b0;
  vector[J] b1;
  vector[J] b2;
  
  vector[C] mu[J];
  
  a0 = theta[,1];
  a1 = theta[,2];
  a2 = theta[,3];
  a3 = theta[,4];
  b3 = theta[,5];
  tau = theta[,6];
  
  b0 = a0 + rows_dot_product(a1,tau) + rows_dot_product(a2,rows_dot_product(tau,tau)) + rows_dot_product(a3,rows_dot_product(tau,rows_dot_product(tau,tau)));
  b1 = a1 + 2*rows_dot_product(a2,tau) + 3*rows_dot_product(a3,rows_dot_product(tau,tau));
  b2 = a2 + 3*rows_dot_product(a3,tau);
  
  for (j in 1:J) {
    mu[j] = C_j[j] * gamma;
  }
  
}


model {
  // Priors
  scale ~ cauchy(0,10);          //
  L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1);      // Set to one for identity matrix (no covariance)
  
  for (j in 1:J) {
    theta[j] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu[j], diag_pre_multiply(scale,L));
  }
  
  for (n in 1:N) {
    if (times[n] < tau[jj[n]]) {
      U[n] ~ normal(a0[jj[n]] + a1[jj[n]]*times[n] + a2[jj[n]]*times[n]^2 + a3[jj[n]]*times[n]^3,sigma);
    } else {
      U[n] ~ normal(b0[jj[n]] + b1[jj[n]]*(times[n]-tau[jj[n]]) + b2[jj[n]]*(times[n]-tau[jj[n]])^2 + b3[jj[n]]*(times[n]-tau[jj[n]])^3,sigma);
    }
  }
}

generated quantities {
  matrix[C,C] Omega;
  matrix[C,C] Sigma_big;
  Omega = multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L);
  Sigma_big = quad_form_diag(Omega, scale);  
}
```


I am calling stan with:
`fit <- stan(file = "./model6-simple.stan", data = regressdata, iter = iterations, pars = "gamma", chains = 1, thin = 10)`

I am not an experienced programmer so please forgive me if the code isn't great. Happy to also supply the dataset and the rest of my R code if required.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling lagging/stopping during execution
parts:
If it fits OK with simulated data and for small data sets,
it's probably just a problem with more data making the posterior
curvature very sharp.

What's probably happening is that adaptation is locking
into a very small step size with a lot of steps and it appears
as if it's frozen (if you look at your process monitor, you'll
probably see it still churning through the compute cycles; if
not let us know).

I didn't know which variable in your model corresponded
to "lines", but if you build big covariance matrices, it
can be very numerically unstable without strong regularization.
This:
> L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1); // Set to one for identity matrix (no covariance)

is putting a uniform distribution over the Cholesky
factors that form correlation matrices. The 1 there
makes it uniform; larger values than 1 concentrate the
mass around the unit correlation matrix.

But if that's not a problem, then you are going to have
to look at either better initialization (for instance, from
a fit with 20 items rather than 150).

There's some opportunities for more efficient coding, but
if it appears locked, just speeding up the code isn't going
to help. If some of these are hierarchical priors, you may
want to use a non-centered parameterization.

Also, having up to a third order (fitting a cubic polynomial)
may not be appropriate for your problem. We know that x, x^2
and x^3 are going to be closely related, so you may wind up
overparameterizing the model.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling lagging/stopping during execution
parts:
Thanks for the reply Bob. The sample is currently at around 7000 samples in 24 hours so nothing patience can't solve. Good to know that this wasn't (entirely) a problem with my code or stan. The "lines" are my J (group) variables. The covariance matrices are only 6 x 6. 

Is there a was to increase the resolution on what sample stan is running during the sampling as opposed to it being broken down into 10 steps (1/10000, 1000/10000, 2000/10000 etc.)?

Thanks for the correction on the Cholesky factors. Admittedly I don't know a huge amount about them and copied this part out of the manual.

Could you give me a one sentence tip on where the coding can be improved? Always keen for development.

I agree this may not be the best model for fitting the data, however we're trying to recreate the results from the aforementioned paper to demonstrate the usefulness of HMC when we can't assume conjugacy. Unfortunately, a lot that is published in our field assumes conjugacy so that a Gibbs sampler can be used, even though often it seems inappropriate to do so (normal error when it is clearly skewed etc.). 

Thanks for your time,

Lachlan

> On Dec 7, 2016, at 8:34 PM, astfalckl <astf...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for the reply Bob. The sample is currently at around 7000 samples in 24 hours so nothing patience can't solve. Good to know that this wasn't (entirely) a problem with my code or stan. The "lines" are my J (group) variables. The covariance matrices are only 6 x 6.

Are you sure you need that many draws? What target effective
sample size are you after and what's the mixing rate
(iterations / n_eff)?
> Is there a was to increase the resolution on what sample stan is running during the sampling as opposed to it being broken down into 10 steps (1/10000, 1000/10000, 2000/10000 etc.)?

Yes, but how to control the refresh rate
depends on the Stan interface.

> Thanks for the correction on the Cholesky factors. Admittedly I don't know a huge amount about them and copied this part out of the manual.
>
> Could you give me a one sentence tip on where the coding can be improved? Always keen for development.

Stan code's like any other code, which means writing
it means knowing how it gets compiled and executed.

> I agree this may not be the best model for fitting the data, however we're trying to recreate the results from the aforementioned paper to demonstrate the usefulness of HMC when we can't assume conjugacy. Unfortunately, a lot that is published in our field assumes conjugacy so that a Gibbs sampler can be used, even though often it seems inappropriate to do so (normal error when it is clearly skewed etc.).

But Gibbs samplers can have problems converging and mixing
even when everything's conjugate. So I hope they're
being careful about monitoring that at least.

- Bob
